claims.text: Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 requires processing temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally processed ZrB2 typically contains holes or pores that initiate degradation during exposure to liquid plating baths.
A chemically homogeneous liquid-precursor route can produce ultrafine ZrB2 nanopowder.
Liquid-precursor-derived ZrB2 can be consolidated into a single-phase ceramic at 1800–1900 °C.
Liquid-precursor-derived ZrB2 can reach near-full densification at 1800–1900 °C.
Pyrolysis generates an in-situ transient liquid intermediate.
The transient liquid intermediate promotes atomic-level mixing and particle rearrangement.
Below 800 °C, the dried precursor undergoes conversion to an intermediate phase.
Chemical homogeneity in the liquid precursor enables intimate mixing of zirconium and boron at the molecular level.
Reduced effective diffusion distances lead to rapid nucleation and growth of ZrB2 with enhanced diffusion kinetics.
Short dwell times during rapid consolidation minimize grain growth.
The proposed route produces a finer and more uniform ZrB2 microstructure than conventional processing.
The proposed microstructure has fewer residual pores and defects than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
The proposed processing route improves grain-boundary cohesion.
Reducing residual pores decreases the number of sites through which the liquid plating bath can penetrate the ceramic.
Reduced liquid penetration improves the strength and structural integrity of ZrB2 during service.
Liquid-precursor-derived ZrB2 will resist crack initiation and failure during prolonged plating-bath exposure better than conventionally processed ZrB2.
The improved ceramic should tolerate tens to hundreds of hours in a service-temperature plating bath without significant microstructural degradation.

contradictions.description: The intervention sample is specified for consolidation at 1800–1900 °C and the conventional sample at above 2300 °C, but the experimental design also says both sets receive identical spark-plasma or pressure-assisted sintering conditions. The thermal conditions therefore cannot be identical as written.
